d319.t: The Call to Come to Me
msg: When the seventy returned from their first mission, they were greatly elated that so many had received the gospel of the kingdom. Jesus rejoiced with them, yet he solemnly warned them against the subtlety of spiritual pride. The words he spoke after that warning are today’s passage: “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧You have entered upon this great work of teaching mortal man that he is a son of God.⟦/Q⟧” The Master did not dampen his disciples’ joy, but he corrected its course so that it would not turn into self-glorification. He turned their eyes from their results to the mission itself, and from the mission to the One who had given it.

This saying sums up the heart of the gospel in a single sentence. The work of the kingdom is not to lay new obligations on people, but to awaken them to the fact that they are already sons and daughters of God. The Urantia Book repeatedly teaches that the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man stand at the center of the gospel of the kingdom (see Paper 170). The moment a person accepts by faith that he is a beloved child of the Universal Father, trust begins to grow within him in place of fear, and belonging in place of isolation. To preach the gospel, then, is not to take the superior stance of one who instructs others, but the humble work of sharing good news with brothers and sisters as children of the same Father. That is why the Master’s warning against spiritual pride stands just before these words.

The Master goes on to urge them, “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧Be not weary in well doing.⟦/Q⟧” Ministry has its joyful days when the fruit is plain to see, but it also has its tedious days when there is no response, and days when we meet misunderstanding and opposition. Just as the seventy were warned not to be puffed up by success, so we must not be discouraged by failure. To leave the results to the Father and simply go on faithfully doing the work entrusted to us is the attitude of a worker in the kingdom. Faithfulness is proven less in brilliant achievements than in steady, day-by-day love. The one who quietly does good where no one notices is the very worker the Master trusts most.

And the Master gives a promise to all who will follow down through the ages: “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧I always stand near, and my invitation-call is, and ever shall be, Come to me all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.⟦/Q⟧” That call was not given only to the people of Galilee two thousand years ago. It is an invitation just as alive for us who read these words today. The Master’s yoke is not a burden that crushes us, but a yoke of love that we bear together as we walk side by side with him.

This invitation is above all a call into relationship. The Master said, “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧Learn of me,⟦/Q⟧” not “Memorize my rules.” To learn of him is to take into our hearts his gentleness and humility and his unwavering trust in the Father. The Spirit of Truth is guiding that learning within us even today.

The Master called himself “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧true and loyal,⟦/Q⟧” and said that those who learn of him “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧shall find spiritual rest for your souls.⟦/Q⟧” This rest does not come from ceasing to work, but from trusting the Father even in the midst of work. On weary days especially, remember this call before your list of things to do. When we come to him and lay down our burdens, we receive strength to do good once more, and we can become people who awaken others to the truth that they too are children of God.
d319.pr: Think of one burden weighing on your heart today, lay it down before the Master, and rest quietly for a while.

msg: At the feast of dedication Jesus was teaching in Solomon’s porch. That morning he had healed Josiah, a man blind from birth, and the Sanhedrin was in session over the charge of Sabbath-breaking. Jesus asked, “⟦Q 164:5.3⟧Many loving works have I shown you from the Father, so that now would I inquire for which one of these good works do you think to stone me?⟦/Q⟧” The Pharisees answered that it was not for any good work, but because “⟦Q 164:5.3⟧you, being a man, dare to make yourself equal with God.⟦/Q⟧” This scene shows that in this final season, as Jesus prepared to leave the world, the hostility of the Jerusalem leaders had already passed the point of no return.

The answer of Jesus is remarkably humble and yet firm: “⟦Q 164:5.3⟧If I do not the works of God, believe me not, but if I do the works of God, even though you believe not in me, I should think you would believe the works.⟦/Q⟧” The Master did not force blind faith on anyone. He offered as evidence the fruits of his life, the deeds of love, mercy, and healing. True faith reveals itself more in the fruits of a life than in words. The Master did not try to win the argument; he simply laid the evidence open so that those with sincere hearts could judge for themselves. This is an attitude we too should follow when we share our faith today.

Then the Master makes the declaration that is the summit of this passage: “⟦Q 164:5.3⟧The Father is in me and I in the Father, and that, as the Father dwells in me, so will I dwell in every one who believes this gospel.⟦/Q⟧” This does not stop at speaking of a privilege belonging to Jesus alone. It is a promise that the intimate oneness of the Father and the Son extends to all who believe. The Urantia Book teaches that the Father personally dwells within us through the Thought Adjuster, and that since Pentecost the Master has come into our hearts as the Spirit of Truth (see Papers 107 and 194).

When we hold fast to this truth, our daily life is changed. God is not One who watches over us from somewhere far off in heaven, but One who is with us in the deepest place of our thoughts and choices. Every small thing we do in love can become the work of the Father who dwells within us. And people will come to recognize the Father by seeing those works rather than by hearing our words. The spiritual life, then, is not a wandering search for a God who is far away, but recognizing the One who is already near and cooperating with him. That process of becoming one with the indwelling Father is the very beginning of our eternal ascent.

The story of Josiah illustrates this truth well. He had not even asked for healing, and his faith was weak, yet after he was cast out of the synagogue he became a follower of the Master. When the religious leaders cast him out, he instead found the true place where God dwells. The experience of being rejected by men can sometimes become a doorway to drawing closer to God.

Those who wanted to stone Jesus had religious zeal, yet they failed to recognize the love of God. Busy defending their theological framework, they could not see the good work done before their very eyes. We too can become trapped in familiar frameworks and miss the new ways in which God is at work. May today be a day of doing his works, aware of the One who dwells within us. A day walked with him is never lonely.
d320.pr: Three times today, pause for a moment and become aware that the Father is within you right now.

msg: In his Sabbath sermon at Pella, Jesus taught his disciples and the multitude, who were soon to face persecution, the way beyond fear. At the center of that teaching is today’s passage. “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies?⟦/Q⟧” And yet, the Master says, not one of them exists without the knowledge of the Father, the source of all life. He warned that the things his enemies were secretly plotting would soon come to light, and at the same time he urged them again and again not to be gripped by fear.

Not even the cheapest bird in the market lies outside the Father’s knowledge. These words show how wide and how detailed is the care of God. The Urantia Book teaches that the Universal Father knows all things, and that his knowledge is not mere information but loving concern (see Paper 3). The passage also says that “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧to the seraphic guardians the very hairs of your head are numbered.⟦/Q⟧” God not only dwells within us personally as the Thought Adjuster, but also cares for the details of our lives through his angels. The smaller and more insignificant a being seems, the more easily it slips from human attention, but it never slips from God’s attention. This is why, however small we may seem, we are never forgotten.

The Master’s question, then, follows naturally: “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧If all of this is true, why should you live in fear of the many trifles which come up in your daily lives?⟦/Q⟧” Our fears usually come less from great disasters than from small things. Tomorrow’s schedule, what others think of us, a minor health concern, the balance in our bank account: such things gnaw at our hearts little by little. The Master gently points out that each of these worries springs from not fully trusting the Father’s love. Fear clouds our judgment and robs us of the strength to love and serve. That is why throughout his public life the Master said so often, “Fear not.”

Of course, these words do not mean that we will suffer no hardship. In the same sermon the Master told his disciples beforehand that they would be brought before the rulers of the synagogues. Sparrows do fall to the ground. But whatever happens, we never fall outside the Father’s knowledge and love. Faith is not a guarantee that there will be no hardship, but the assurance that we are not forsaken in the midst of it. Indeed, hardship can lead us to grasp the Father’s hand all the more tightly.

This trust is not lazy resignation. To entrust things to the Father does not mean leaving undone what we should do, but laying down our anxiety about the outcome after we have done our best. A life that prepares wisely yet is not bound by worry: this is the freedom enjoyed by the children of God. In each such moment of trust, the Thought Adjuster draws our souls a little further toward the Father. Walk through this day holding in your heart this identity as a child of the Father.

Finally the Master declares, “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧Fear not; you are of much more value than many sparrows.⟦/Q⟧” Our worth comes not from our achievements or possessions but from the fact that we are children of the Father. Each time worry floods in today, recall these words. As the practice of entrusting small things to the Father accumulates, a peace grows that stands unshaken even before great trials.
d321.pr: Write down one small worry troubling you today, and entrust it to the Father, remembering that he knows.

msg: Peter asked whether the Master’s parable of the watchful servants applied only to the apostles or to all the disciples. In answering this question, the Master spoke today’s words: “⟦Q 165:6.2⟧In the time of testing, a man’s soul is revealed; trial discloses what really is in the heart.⟦/Q⟧” These words were meant not only for the apostles but for every believer who had entered the kingdom. The call to be watchful does not belong only to those who hold some special office.

On peaceful days everyone looks faithful. When all goes smoothly, it is not hard to confess our faith and act with goodness. But when difficulty comes, when we suffer loss or are misunderstood or lose someone we love, what lay hidden within us comes to light. Some reveal resentment and fear; others reveal, even then, an astonishing patience and trust. Trial does not so much create something new as bring clearly into view what was already within us. Trial is therefore like a mirror that lets us know ourselves. Before that mirror we discover that we are weaker than we thought, or perhaps stronger than we thought. That is why the depth of faith shows itself more clearly on the rough road than on the smooth one.

The Master says that when the servant is tested and proved, the lord of the house may set such a servant over his household and trust him with the care of his children. And he says, “⟦Q 165:6.2⟧Likewise, will I soon know who can be trusted with the welfare of my children when I shall have returned to the Father.⟦/Q⟧” These words looked ahead to the final week in Jerusalem that was soon to come. In fact, the apostles were scattered and stumbled in that trial, but those who rose again became the ones entrusted with the work of the kingdom. How we rise after falling matters more than the fall itself. Peter denied the Master three times, yet he returned and became one who strengthened his brethren.

The Urantia Book teaches that the difficulties we meet are not mere chance suffering but opportunities to discipline character. Courage grows only where there is danger, patience only where there is delay, and faith only where there is uncertainty (see Paper 3). Trial, then, is not proof that God has abandoned us, but the process by which we are prepared to bear a greater trust. God does not deliberately send us trials, but he can turn every trial we meet into material for growth.

The faithful steward is not a servant who works only while his master is watching. In the same discourse the Master warned of the servant who grows slothful, thinking that his lord delays his coming. The one who goes on unchanged in the work entrusted to him, even in hours when no one sees and results are slow in coming, is the one who has truly been proved. The heavenly Father never forgets such faithfulness.

If there is a time of testing in your life today, do not merely try to escape it; look honestly at what it reveals. Even if you see something disappointing, there is no need to lose heart. A weakness brought to light becomes a starting point for its correction. Remember the Master’s promise to exalt in the affairs of his kingdom those who endure the trials of this hour, and choose faithfulness in today’s small trials. The small inconveniences and disappointments you face today are precious opportunities to practice faithfulness.
d322.pr: Reflect on what a recent difficulty revealed in your heart, and decide how you will respond next time.

msg: On the way to Philadelphia, Thomas asked Jesus about accidents and calamities. People in those days believed that prosperity was a sign of God’s approval and adversity the proof of his displeasure. Jesus declared such belief to be superstition, and then spoke today’s passage: “⟦Q 166:4.4⟧The Father causes his rain to fall on the just and the unjust; the sun likewise shines on the righteous and the unrighteous.⟦/Q⟧” The Master understood the confusion of the apostles, who had long carried this question, and he wished to correct the mistaken idea handed down from their fathers.

The Master cites two events everyone knew at the time: Pilate’s mingling the blood of certain Galileans with their sacrifices, and the fall of the tower of Siloam that killed eighteen men. People whispered that those who suffered such things must have committed especially great sins. But Jesus says plainly that they were not sinners above their fellows; “⟦Q 166:4.4⟧these folks were simply innocent victims of one of the accidents of time.⟦/Q⟧” These words must have shocked his hearers. To people who saw the will of God as the direct cause of every event, the teaching that there are also chance accidents in the world was strange and new.

This teaching brings us deep comfort and release today as well. When we fall ill, have an accident, or fail in business, we find ourselves blaming ourselves and asking what we did wrong to be punished. Or seeing another’s misfortune, we quietly judge that he must have done something wrong. The Urantia Book teaches that the material world operates according to natural law, and that God does not arbitrarily suspend those laws. Accidents are not God’s punishments but things that happen in an evolving world (see Paper 86). The habit of interpreting misfortune as divine punishment lays a double burden on those who suffer, for it adds guilt and shame on top of their pain. The Master sought to free people from that burden.

Yet this does not mean that God is indifferent. The Father does not manipulate each material event, but he is always present beside our souls as we pass through those events. His care shows itself less in preventing accidents than in helping us grow spiritually and recover in the midst of them. That is why, passing through the same disaster, some come away with deeper faith and compassion. He comforts our wounded hearts and gives us wisdom and courage to rise again from the place where we fell.

The parable of the barren fig tree that the Master told next shows another side of this teaching. Accidents are not punishment, yet our lives are still called to bear fruit. Rather than sitting in judgment on the misfortunes of others, the wise person looks to his own life and strives to bear spiritual fruit.

Today, when you meet a neighbor who is suffering, stand beside him rather than inquiring into the cause. And when you yourself meet with hardship, do not shut yourself up in needless guilt. Just as the rain and the sunshine fall alike upon all, so the Father’s love falls without partiality upon all his children. The one who trusts that love does not lose his eternal security even before the accidents of time. That trust sets us free from fear and superstition.
d323.pr: Rather than judging someone who is suffering misfortune, pray for them or offer them a word of comfort today.

msg: At Jericho, after speaking of the blessedness of marriage and children, Jesus blessed the little children whom their mothers had brought to him. At that time the Master also taught about cultivating in children the habit of divine worship, and today’s passage holds the heart of that teaching. When it is not possible to worship God in the tabernacles of nature, men should do their best to provide houses of beauty, “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧sanctuaries of appealing simplicity and artistic embellishment.⟦/Q⟧” It is a most delicate insight into the influence that a place of worship has upon the human heart.

The passage says that “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧truth, beauty, and holiness are powerful and effective aids to true worship.⟦/Q⟧” Throughout the Urantia Book, truth, beauty, and goodness appear again and again as three paths leading to God (see Paper 56). Beauty is not mere decoration but a channel that lifts our hearts toward God. That is why we spontaneously feel awe as we gaze at a sunset or stand in a quiet forest. Before beauty the soul forgets itself and opens toward a higher reality. Worship, therefore, is not a matter of the intellect alone, but the response of our whole being to God, emotions and senses included.

But the passage at once restores the balance. “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧Spirit communion is not promoted by mere massive ornateness and overmuch embellishment with man’s elaborate and ostentatious art.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧Beauty is most religious when it is most simple and naturelike.⟦/Q⟧” Grand buildings and costly ornament can actually turn people’s eyes away from God toward human achievement. True beauty is a humble beauty that leads us to God rather than displaying itself. The simpler the place of worship, the more wholly our hearts are gathered to God alone.

This passage shows a special and deep concern for little children. “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧How unfortunate that little children should have their first introduction to concepts of public worship in cold and barren rooms,⟦/Q⟧” the passage laments. “⟦Q 167:6.6⟧The child should be introduced to worship in nature’s outdoors.⟦/Q⟧” It is an important responsibility of parents and teachers to see that a child’s first impression of God is one of wonder and joy rather than boredom or fear. The first experiences of childhood shape a lifetime of religious sensitivity.

This teaching applies to each of our own lives of worship as well. How are we tending the place where we pray and meditate? A special space is not strictly necessary, but simple beauty that quiets the heart, a small potted plant by the window, a tidy desk, soft music, helps our communion with God. Above all, the finest sanctuary is nature itself, which God has made. In the sky and the trees and the wind we meet the Father’s handiwork without any ornament at all. As the small habit of meeting God at the same place and the same hour each day accumulates, that place quietly becomes our own holy sanctuary.

Today, step outside even for a moment, look upon the world God has made, and let your heart turn to worship. And if you have children or young neighbors, offer some small help so that they may first meet God in joy and beauty. When truth, beauty, and holiness come together, worship becomes not a duty but the joy of the soul. Worship offered in this way renews our souls.
d324.pr: Step outside for a moment today, gaze at the beauty of nature, and offer the Father a silent worship of thanksgiving.

d325.t: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
msg: On the fourth day after Lazarus died, Jesus arrived at Bethany. Martha met the Master on the road and said through her tears that had he been there, her brother would not have died. In that moment full of grief and disappointment, Jesus looked straight into the eyes of Martha and said: “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he dies, yet shall he live. In truth, whosoever lives and believes in me shall never really die.⟦/Q⟧” And he asked, “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧Martha, do you believe this?⟦/Q⟧” This question was not meant to test Martha, but was a loving question meant to awaken the faith that lay sleeping deep in her heart.

Before performing the miracle of raising Lazarus, the Master first awakened Martha’s faith. The weight of these words is greater even than what was about to happen at the tomb. Lazarus came back to life, but later he did in the end meet bodily death. The life the Master spoke of, however, is not the prolonging of the flesh but eternal survival, the life of a God-knowing soul that goes on living beyond death. This saying, then, is a promise not to Lazarus alone but to all who believe in the Master. To the grieving he gave first not an explanation but himself.

The Urantia Book teaches that after death human beings awaken on the mansion worlds and continue the journey of ascent (see Paper 47). The soul of one who has accepted sonship with God by faith grows together with the Thought Adjuster, and even when the body falls, the identity of that soul is preserved. When the Master said that such a one “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧shall never really die,⟦/Q⟧” he was pointing to this very truth. Bodily death is not the end but the threshold of passage into a higher life. Every moment in which we now grow in knowing and loving God is the first chapter of that eternal life. Death cannot cut that story short.

Martha’s answer is beautiful too: “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧Yes, I have long believed that you are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God, even he who should come to this world.⟦/Q⟧” Martha was a busy and practical woman, and she had once received a gentle rebuke from the Master. Yet in the moment of her deepest sorrow, she confessed an unwavering faith. Faith shines all the brighter when it is not the feeling of a calm hour but a choice made in the very midst of grief and questioning. Her confession is all the more precious because it came before the Master had yet worked any miracle.

We too cannot escape fear and sorrow when we lose someone we love or contemplate our own death. Jesus himself wept before the tomb of Lazarus. To grieve does not mean to lack faith. But the sorrow of one who has faith is sorrow within hope. We know that parting is not forever, and that we will meet again in the next world and walk the path of ascent together. That hope does not remove our sorrow, but it holds us so that sorrow does not turn into despair.

Today the Master asks us the question he asked Martha: Do you believe this? Do not hesitate before this question; answer it from the depths of your heart. Eternal life does not begin only after death; it has already begun here and now, in knowing God. Walk on, enjoying that life in the midst of today. In that life we can live boldly, without fear of death.
d325.pr: Write a short confession answering in your own words the Master’s question, “⟦Q 168:0.7⟧Do you believe this?⟦/Q⟧”

msg: On the way from Bethany to Pella after the raising of Lazarus, the apostles asked many questions about prayer and its answers. The Master had not responded at once to the message sent by Martha and Mary, yet in the end he had answered in a far greater way, and this left deep questions in their minds. Jesus replied to their questions with ten teachings, and today’s passage is the last two of them. They wanted to know why God answers some prayers at once and remains long silent before others.

The ninth teaching says, “⟦Q 168:4.12⟧Do not hesitate to pray the prayers of spirit longing; doubt not that you shall receive the answer to your petitions.⟦/Q⟧” Yet these answers “⟦Q 168:4.12⟧will be on deposit, awaiting your achievement of those future spiritual levels of actual cosmic attainment.⟦/Q⟧” This is a truly remarkable teaching. The sincere prayers we have offered never vanish; they are kept until we have grown enough to receive their answers. Whether on this world or on others, we will one day recognize the long-waiting answers. Sincere prayers are laid up one by one in heaven’s keeping, awaiting us.

The tenth teaching declares, “⟦Q 168:4.13⟧All genuine spirit-born petitions are certain of an answer.⟦/Q⟧” The promise “⟦Q 168:4.13⟧Ask and you shall receive⟦/Q⟧” does not change. But because we are “⟦Q 168:4.13⟧progressive creatures of time and space,⟦/Q⟧” we must constantly reckon with the time-space factor in the experience of receiving our answers. Just as a seed needs seasons to become fruit, so spiritual answers unfold according to our growth and in their proper time. There is no need, then, to conclude that our prayers are in vain because the answer is delayed.

The important distinction here is between prayers offered from spirit longing and requests born of material desire. Other teachings in the same discourse say that only prayers born of the spirit and nurtured by faith can be answered. Prayers that ask to draw nearer to God, to receive strength to love, to grasp the truth, are always answered. But that answer may take a different shape from what we expected, and it is often far greater and deeper than we imagined. When we trust the wisdom of the Father, who gives us what we need rather than what we asked, prayer becomes not demand but communion.

So do not lose heart when your prayers seem to go unanswered. Delay is not denial. As in the case of Lazarus, God’s delay is sometimes the preparation for a better answer. When we have matured enough to receive that answer, we will know that God never for a moment forgot our petitions. The Thought Adjuster remembers every sincere longing we have offered. Even while we wait for the answer, do not forget that in prayer we are already with the Father.

If today there is a prayer you have long offered without seeing an answer, lay it once more before the Father. But this time, rather than pressing for the outcome, ask also that you may grow into one who can receive that answer. The one who prays in this way turns even the season of waiting into a season of growth. Waiting is never in vain.
d326.pr: Offer once more a prayer you have long been waiting on, and ask also that you may grow enough to receive its answer.

msg: In his last teaching at Pella, Jesus told three stories: of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. When the Pharisees criticized the Master for associating with publicans and sinners, he answered them with these stories that reveal what kind of God God is. Today’s passage is the introduction, and it holds the central truth running through all three stories. Each of them is a story of seeking what was lost, and of rejoicing together once it is found.

The Master first acknowledges the teaching of the prophets. “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧You have been admonished by the prophets from Samuel to John that you should seek for God — search for truth. Always have they said, ‘Seek the Lord while he may be found.’⟦/Q⟧” This teaching remains true and should be taken to heart. But the Master goes one step further: “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧I have come to show you that, while you are seeking to find God, God is likewise seeking to find you.⟦/Q⟧” This is the new face of God that Jesus revealed.

For a long time human religion was understood as man’s effort to climb up in search of God. People believed that only by offering sacrifices, keeping rituals, and observing the law could they draw near to God. But Jesus reversed the direction. God is not One who sits with folded arms waiting for us to come to him, but One who goes out first in search of us, like the shepherd who roams the hills and fields to find his lost sheep. The Urantia Book teaches that the very indwelling of the Thought Adjuster within us is proof that God has come to us first (see Paper 107). Our salvation does not begin with our straining to lay hold of God, but with God first laying hold of us. Our part is not to shake off that hand but to receive it in faith.

The passage says, “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧There is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over the ninety and nine just persons who need no repentance.⟦/Q⟧” And it adds, “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧The fact that souls are lost only increases the interest of the heavenly Father.⟦/Q⟧” What comforting words these are! When we drift away and fail, God does not turn from us in disappointment; rather he seeks us with even greater interest. Our straying does not diminish God’s love but reveals it all the more. There is no need to fear coming before God because of the memory of our sins and failures.

The Master acknowledged that it had truly been said of the Son of Man that “⟦Q 169:1.2⟧he is a friend of publicans and sinners.⟦/Q⟧” He gladly took as his own name the words that had been hurled at him as an accusation. This is a challenge to us as well. Are we becoming friends of the lost and of those pushed to the margins of society, or, like the Pharisees, are we keeping our distance and passing judgment? Those who know the heart of God join in the work of seeking the lost. The heart of the shepherd searching for his lost sheep must now become the heart of us who follow him.

If today you feel that you have drifted away from God, do not think the way back too hard. Before we can even take a single step, the Father is already running toward us. And having experienced that love, we must become people who go out with the same love toward the lost neighbors around us. That is the gratitude of those who have been found.
d327.pr: Think of someone who has grown distant, and reach out first today with a short message asking how they are.

msg: In his last sermon at Pella, Jesus taught comprehensively about the kingdom of heaven. Today’s passage comes from the part dealing with the relationship between the kingdom and righteousness: “⟦Q 170:3.9⟧The righteousness of any act must be measured by the motive; the highest forms of good are therefore unconscious.⟦/Q⟧” These words make plain God’s point of view, which looks at the heart that gives rise to an act rather than at the outward act itself. They move religion from a list of outward deeds to a matter of inward motive.

The Jewish religion of that day regarded the keeping of the detailed provisions of the law as righteousness. How many steps one might walk on the Sabbath, what foods one might eat, these were the measure of righteousness. But the passage says that “⟦Q 170:3.9⟧Jesus was never concerned with morals or ethics as such.⟦/Q⟧” The Master was wholly concerned with “⟦Q 170:3.9⟧that inward and spiritual fellowship with God the Father which so certainly and directly manifests itself as outward and loving service for man.⟦/Q⟧” Righteousness is not keeping rules; it is love alive and in motion. The provisions of the law were used to judge people, but love is used to serve them.

The saying that the highest forms of good are unconscious is worth pondering deeply. The person who is always conscious, while doing good, that he is doing good has not yet made that goodness his own nature. Mature love does not calculate or boast; it flows out as naturally as breathing. This is also what the Master meant when he said not to let the left hand know what the right hand is doing. A soul transformed in deep fellowship with God does good without even knowing it. Spiritual growth, then, is not piling up more good deeds, but being transformed into a person from whom good deeds flow of themselves.

The passage also says that “⟦Q 170:3.9⟧the religion of the kingdom is a genuine personal experience which no man can contain within himself.⟦/Q⟧” The one who truly knows God cannot keep that experience to himself. The consciousness of being a member of the family of believers leads inevitably to the service of one’s brothers and sisters. Personal faith and social service are not two things but one life showing itself inwardly and outwardly. The deeper the inward fellowship, the richer the outward service. The joy of knowing God does not shrink when shared; it only grows.

This teaching leads us to look again at our daily lives. What are we hoping for when we do good? Some good deeds are done to win recognition, out of a sense of duty, or to ease a feeling of guilt. Such deeds are not without meaning, but what God desires is a love that wells up from a deeper place. That love cannot be manufactured by force; it grows in fellowship with the Father. God looks not only at results but at the direction of the heart, and he rejoices in the sincere love contained even in clumsy deeds.

So before striving to do more good deeds, first spend time with the Father. When we receive God’s love deeply in worship and meditation, that love overflows of itself toward our neighbors. When the motive becomes clear, the deeds set themselves right. A single small kindness that comes from a heart so cleansed is counted in heaven as the greatest righteousness.
d328.pr: Do one good thing today, quietly, without telling anyone.

msg: After setting forth the Master’s sermon on the kingdom of heaven at Pella, the author of the Urantia Book looks back on how the concept of the kingdom has changed through history. The ideal of a spiritual brotherhood that Jesus taught has for the most part gone unrealized, and an outward church has taken its place. After this sober assessment, today’s passage begins with a powerful declaration: “⟦Q 170:5.21⟧Mistake not! there is in the teachings of Jesus an eternal nature which will not permit them forever to remain unfruitful in the hearts of thinking men.⟦/Q⟧” Truth may be veiled for a while, but it cannot be buried forever.

The passage calls the church “⟦Q 170:5.21⟧only the larval stage of the thwarted spiritual kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” And it says that the church has become “⟦Q 170:5.21⟧the cocoon in which the kingdom of Jesus’ concept now slumbers.⟦/Q⟧” This image is both a criticism and a hope. A cocoon looks like a prison confining life, yet in truth a transformation is being prepared within it. Although the church falls short of Jesus’ original ideal, it has served to preserve his teachings and carry them through this material age into the next. Within the church, too, countless people have followed the Master with sincere faith, and their devotion has carried these teachings down to our own day.

The Urantia Book acknowledges that it was natural and necessary for the church to arise as the social outgrowth of the kingdom (see Paper 170, section 5). The trouble was not that the church came into being, but that the church took the place of the kingdom itself. As the living brotherhood of spirit-born individuals hardened into institutions, doctrines, and rituals, the spiritual freedom and personal experience Jesus envisioned were pushed into the background. Yet the seed did not die. The hardening of living faith into rigid forms is a danger repeated in every age and every religion.

The passage promises that “⟦Q 170:5.21⟧the kingdom of the divine brotherhood is still alive and will eventually and certainly come forth from this long submergence, just as surely as the butterfly eventually emerges as the beautiful unfolding of its less attractive creature of metamorphic development.⟦/Q⟧” This shows God’s patience with history. God does not hurry, but neither does he ever give up. The teachings of Jesus awaken again in every age within those of sincere heart, and one day they will come to full flower in a more spiritual dispensation. The age in which we live is also part of that long transformation, and we have our own part to play in it.

This word asks two things of us today. One is that we not fall into cynicism even as we see the limitations of religious institutions. Merely condemning the cocoon will not bring forth the butterfly. The other is that each of us become a place where that butterfly awakens. The kingdom of Jesus begins in the individual heart before it begins in any outward organization. As a living relationship with the Father and brotherly love toward our neighbors grow within us, the slumbering kingdom awakens little by little. The Spirit of Truth is even now seeking sincere hearts and raising up the kingdom anew within them.

Today, do not merely keep the teachings of Jesus as a tradition, but receive them as living experience. When each one of us lives out the Master’s original gospel, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, the cocoon will open and the kingdom will spread its wings once more. Those wings unfold from our own small faithfulness.
d329.pr: Choose one teaching of Jesus to put into practice in your life today, and keep it throughout the day.

d330.t: Why Would You Be a Disciple?
msg: On the road to Jerusalem after leaving the Pella encampment, a multitude of almost a thousand followed Jesus. Many expected that the Master would at last establish the kingdom in Jerusalem and ascend the throne. Just before this, Salome, the mother of James and John, had even asked that her two sons might sit at the Master’s right hand and left. In this atmosphere Jesus halted at the ford of the Jordan and told them to count the cost of becoming his disciples. Today’s passage is the conclusion of that discourse.

The Master first tells them, “⟦Q 171:2.5⟧Now should you examine yourself to find out your motive for being my disciple.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 171:2.5⟧If you seek honor and glory, if you are worldly minded, you are like the salt when it has lost its savor.⟦/Q⟧” The value of salt lies in its saltiness. Salt that has lost its savor is good for nothing. In the same way, a disciple lacking pure love for the kingdom of God cannot give the kingdom its savor, however zealously he may follow. He may look like salt, yet he has lost the very essence of salt. Just as salt dissolves into food and gives it flavor, the disciple must not lose the character of the kingdom even while living mingled with the world.

Then the Master solemnly warns them: “I have warned you to turn back to your homes in peace if you are not willing to drink with me the cup which is being prepared.” This cup was the cup of the suffering, rejection, and death that were soon to come. The Master did not hold people against their will. Rather, he spoke honestly so that they might choose knowing clearly what they were agreeing to. True discipleship is not emotional enthusiasm but a conscious decision to follow even when the cost is known.

The Master lamented, “⟦Q 171:2.5⟧Again and again have I told you that my kingdom is not of this world, but you will not believe me.⟦/Q⟧” People heard only what they wanted to hear. When Jesus spoke of a spiritual kingdom, they still imagined a political one. His closing words, “⟦Q 171:2.5⟧He who has ears to hear let him hear,⟦/Q⟧” mean that the truth had already been proclaimed, but receiving it was each person’s own part. We too must ask whether, as we read the Bible or the Urantia Book, we are picking out only the parts that suit our expectations. Truth often comes not to confirm our expectations but to correct them.

What is our motive for walking the path of faith today? It may be peace of mind, blessing and success, recognition within the community, or the assurance of eternal life. Such hopes may have drawn us at first, and there is nothing shameful in that. But as faith grows, our motives too must be purified. At last we come to follow not in order to gain something, but because loving God and doing his will is itself our joy. The purifying of motive is not finished all at once; it takes place through a lifelong cooperation with the Thought Adjuster.

The Master’s way is not an easy way, yet those who walked it to the end found a joy they would not exchange for any glory of this world. Sit quietly for a while today and examine honestly the motives of your faith. Then ask the Father to make your heart purer. Like salt that does not lose its savor, our lives will give the world the savor of the kingdom of God.
d330.pr: Write down three motives for which you walk the path of faith, and choose the purest among them.

msg: At Jericho, Jesus stopped at the cry of the blind beggar Bartimeus, and he called Zaccheus, the chief of the publicans, down from the sycamore tree and stayed in his house. After recording these two events, the Urantia Book devotes a separate section to the things Jesus did as he passed by. Many of the most important things in the Master’s life happened not at planned gatherings but along the way. Today’s passage is the portion that best reveals the personality of Jesus. His ministry took place not only from the pulpit but on the road, at the table, and beside the well.

The passage first says, “⟦Q 171:7.5⟧Jesus was never in a hurry.⟦/Q⟧” The Master’s final weeks were busier and more urgent than anyone’s. He knew of the suffering that awaited him in Jerusalem, and there was much he still had to teach. Yet “⟦Q 171:7.5⟧he had time to comfort his fellow men ‘as he passed by.’⟦/Q⟧” Not being in a hurry does not mean being slow; it means not missing the person who stands before you now. For the Master, people always came before schedules.

The passage also says that he always made his friends feel at ease, that “⟦Q 171:7.5⟧he was a charming listener,⟦/Q⟧” and that he never engaged in the meddlesome probing of the souls of his associates. Many people who say they are helping others are in fact advising, teaching, and prying. But the Master listened deeply first. He waited until the other opened his heart of his own accord, and he respected the private domain of that soul. Only where there is such respect does a person feel safe and able to speak the truth. Listening demands a greater love than speaking, for we must empty ourselves for a while and enter the world of the other.

The most beautiful words in the passage are these: “⟦Q 171:7.5⟧the recipients of his mercy did not so much feel that they were confessing to him as that they were conferring with him.⟦/Q⟧” In the Master’s presence people became not sinners standing before a judgment seat but respected companions. And “⟦Q 171:7.5⟧they had unbounded confidence in him because they saw he had so much faith in them.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus believed in people. He looked not at what they were at present, but at the spirit of the Father within them and at what they could become. The experience of someone believing in us is one of the most powerful forces for changing a person.

This teaching casts new light on our everyday relationships. Always pleading busyness, we miss the small signals of those beside us. We pass by a coworker’s tired face, a family member’s brief sigh, a friend’s hesitant trailing words. To live as the Master lived begins less with drawing up grand plans for service than with giving our full attention to the people we meet today. Simply by listening well, we can become a great comfort to someone. Hurry is the enemy of love, for when the heart is rushed, people look like obstacles to our work.

When you plan your day today, leave some room in your heart along with your list of things to do. In that open space you will meet the people God sends to you. And rather than judging or trying to fix them, first believe in them and listen to them. What Jesus did as he passed by, we too can do along our own way.
d331.pr: Listen to one person you meet today all the way to the end, without interrupting.

msg: On the Sabbath evening six days before the Passover, a feast was given for Jesus and Lazarus at the house of Simon in Bethany. As the feast was drawing to a close, Mary the sister of Lazarus came with a flask of very costly ointment, poured it over the Master’s head and feet, and wiped his feet with her hair. The whole house was filled with its fragrance, but some, especially Judas Iscariot, murmured that the ointment should have been sold and the money given to the poor. Today’s passage is the Master’s reply to that murmuring. Their words sounded reasonable, yet they chilled the beauty of the moment.

Jesus put his hand upon Mary’s head as she knelt by his side and, with a kindly expression upon his face, said, “⟦Q 172:1.6⟧Let her alone, every one of you. Why do you trouble her about this, seeing that she has done a good thing in her heart?⟦/Q⟧” The Master saw this act not as waste but as a good thing that came from the heart. Others reckoned the price of the ointment, but the Master saw the love it held. God looks not at the market value of our deeds but at the sincerity of the heart that gives rise to them. Mary expressed, with the most precious thing she had, a gratitude and love that words could not fully say.

The Master did not take lightly the work of helping the poor. He simply said, “⟦Q 172:1.6⟧You have the poor always with you so that you may minister to them at any time it seems good to you; but I shall not always be with you.⟦/Q⟧” There is a love that can be given only in this present moment. Mary believed in the Master’s death and departure, which the other apostles could never bring themselves to accept, and out of that faith she prepared this anointing. That is why the Master said that by this act Mary had reproved them all. Love has its time. There is a love that, once its moment is missed, can never be expressed in the same way again.

This scene shows the age-old tension between love and practicality. Judas’s words seemed on the surface reasonable and even pious. But the Urantia Book tells us that by that time Judas’s heart was already darkening with wounded feelings and disappointment. Criticism that sounds plausible on the surface can in fact come from a heart dried up of love. On the other hand, a devotion that looks excessive to others may be the most beautiful worship before God. Before criticizing another’s devotion, we should first ask whether our own hearts are warm enough to understand it.

The Master promised that “⟦Q 172:1.6⟧wherever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will be spoken of in memory of her.⟦/Q⟧” And indeed, two thousand years later we are still reading Mary’s story. Not some great achievement or a great sermon, but one woman’s quiet act of love is remembered forever. In the kingdom of God greatness is measured not by size but by the sincerity of love. God does not forget a single one of our hidden acts of love.

Today let us also offer a love that does not calculate. Whether it is time given to God or devoted care given to someone we love, offer it with your whole heart rather than weighing its efficiency. And when you see someone’s heartfelt devotion, do not be quick to judge it. The Master may be catching in it a fragrance that we cannot perceive.
d332.pr: Without weighing efficiency, offer one act of devoted care today, with your whole heart, to God or to someone you love.

msg: On the Sunday that Jesus entered Jerusalem riding on a colt, the multitude cheered and cried hosanna. But as evening came on and the crowds dispersed, Jesus and his immediate followers were left alone in the temple courts. “⟦Q 172:4.2⟧What a strange day it had been!⟦/Q⟧” the passage says. The apostles were thoughtful, but speechless. In that quiet moment they sat down by the treasury, watching the people drop in their contributions, and there the Master called their attention to a poor widow. In the place where the splendid procession had passed, the Master set his heart instead upon the smallest of scenes.

The rich put much into the receiving box, and all gave something in accordance with the extent of their possessions. Then a poor widow, scantily attired, came along and cast in two mites, the smallest of coins. It was a scene no one would have noticed. But Jesus declared, “⟦Q 172:4.2⟧This poor widow cast in more than all the others.⟦/Q⟧” For all the others, from their superfluity, cast in some trifle, but she, even though she was in want, gave all that she had, even her living. She could never have imagined that she would be praised.

These words show that God’s reckoning is altogether different from man’s. Man looks at the amount, but God looks at the proportion, or more exactly, at the heart. What is given from abundance, however large, costs the giver nothing. But the widow gave her all. Her devotion held complete trust in God. Rather than worrying about what she would eat tomorrow, she entrusted herself to God. That very trust made those tiny coins the greatest offering in heaven.

It is deeply meaningful that this scene comes on the evening of the day of the triumphal entry. During the day great crowds had spread their garments on the road and waved palm branches. But the Urantia Book tells us that this enthusiasm was superficial, and that the same multitude would soon reject him. One woman’s quiet devotion weighs more before God than the loudest acclaim. True faith shows itself not amid the shouts of the crowd but in small devotions offered where no one sees. God measures not the volume of the shouting but the depth of the heart.

This teaching is a great comfort when we feel we have little to give. We may think that we have no great wealth, no outstanding talent, no abundance of time. But God does not compare what we have with what others have. When we sincerely offer the little we have, it is never small before God. Those who have much, on the other hand, should ask themselves whether they are giving only from their abundance. The worth of a gift lies not in how much is left over, but in how precious to us was the thing we gave.

Consider today what your two mites might be, to offer for God and your neighbor. It may be money, but it may also be an hour set apart from a busy day, or a kind word spoken from a weary body. The Father sees that small devotion as more precious than anyone else does, and he remembers it. That is our two mites.
d333.pr: Willingly give something today, for God and your neighbor, that feels a little costly given your circumstances.

msg: On Monday, the day after he entered Jerusalem, Jesus intended to teach in the temple courts. But the place was as noisy as a market with the cries of cattle dealers and the haggling of money-changers. Pilgrims had to buy animals for sacrifice at outrageous prices and pay high fees to exchange their money for temple currency. The profits went to the powerful men of the temple. Before this spectacle Jesus took up a whip and drove the merchants and the animals out of the temple. Today’s passage explains what this event discloses. It was not an act swept along by anger, but a righteous decision reached after deep reflection.

The passage first says that this cleansing of the temple “⟦Q 173:1.11⟧discloses the Master’s attitude toward commercializing the practices of religion as well as his detestation of all forms of unfairness and profiteering at the expense of the poor and the unlearned.⟦/Q⟧” The Master was ordinarily gentle and patient, but he never let it pass when the weak were exploited in the name of religion. To profit by taking advantage of the devout hearts of poor pilgrims seeking to approach God was to dishonor God. The Master’s indignation was never for himself, but always for the wounded neighbor.

The passage goes on to make plain an important principle: Jesus “⟦Q 173:1.11⟧did not look with approval upon the refusal to employ force to protect the majority of any given human group against the unfair and enslaving practices of unjust minorities who may be able to entrench themselves behind political, financial, or ecclesiastical power.⟦/Q⟧” This balanced explanation keeps us from misunderstanding Jesus’ teaching of nonresistance. The Master taught us to turn the other cheek to personal insult, but he never taught us to stand by while helpless neighbors are systematically exploited. This event, then, should be read not as a justification of violence, but as an awakening to love’s responsibility toward the weak.

The last sentence weighs especially heavily: “⟦Q 173:1.11⟧Shrewd, wicked, and designing men are not to be permitted to organize themselves for the exploitation and oppression of those who, because of their idealism, are not disposed to resort to force for self-protection.⟦/Q⟧” For good people to let evil run rampant because they are too naive or too passive is itself a kind of evasion of responsibility. Love is gentle, but never weak. True love knows how to stand up firmly to protect the weak.

This teaching leads us today to consider the relationship between faith and social justice. When religion becomes an instrument of money and power, the place that should be purest becomes the most defiled. In the communities to which we belong and the places where we work, we should watch whether the weak are being treated unjustly. And when we see it, it is the responsibility of a citizen of the kingdom not to keep silent but to strive to set it right by wise and just means. Our small courage can become a great shield for someone.

At the same time, this event leads us to look at the temple of our own hearts. Is our inner life, where God dwells, filled with the noise of calculation, gain, and greed? Today ask the Master to cleanse the courts of your heart. And with a cleansed heart, ask for the courage to stand on the side of the weak among your neighbors who are being exploited. That is the Master’s justice.
d334.pr: Look around you for someone weak who is being treated unjustly, and find one thing you can do for them.

msg: On Tuesday morning, before going to the temple, Peter and James asked Jesus about the forgiveness of sin. For several days the two of them had been debating the differences in the Master’s teaching about God’s forgiveness. Jesus explained God’s forgiveness to them in the light of the relationship between a father and his child. Because the father understands his child deeply, he said, forgiveness is inherent in him. Today’s passage is the portion in which he extends that teaching to the relationships between one person and another. This teaching transforms not only our relationship with God but also our relationships with one another.

The Master says, “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧When a wise man understands the inner impulses of his fellows, he will love them.⟦/Q⟧” And he says, “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧When you love your brother, you have already forgiven him.⟦/Q⟧” Forgiveness is not a resolution squeezed out by force, but a fruit that flows naturally from understanding and love. When we cannot forgive someone, it is usually because we see only their actions and fail to see the hurt, fear, and immaturity behind them. The more deeply we understand, the less room there is for hatred. The starting point of forgiveness, then, is understanding more than willpower.

The Master says that “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧this capacity to understand man’s nature and forgive his apparent wrongdoing is Godlike.⟦/Q⟧” Wise parents love, understand, and forgive their children even when transient misunderstanding has apparently separated them. The child, being immature, may feel a sense of guilty separation from a father’s full approval, “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧but the true father is never conscious of any such separation.⟦/Q⟧” The words “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧sin is an experience of creature consciousness; it is not a part of God’s consciousness⟦/Q⟧” are a wonderful comfort. Even when we feel that we have drifted away, the Father has not drifted away from us.

The Master goes on to say, “⟦Q 174:1.5⟧Your inability or unwillingness to forgive your fellows is the measure of your immaturity.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 174:1.5⟧You hold grudges and nurse vengefulness in direct proportion to your ignorance of the inner nature and true longings of your children and your fellow beings.⟦/Q⟧” These words remind us that resentment springs as much from our own lack of understanding as from the other’s wrongdoing. An unforgiving heart keeps us bound to the past and blocks our spiritual growth. Maturity is the growing ability to understand more broadly and deeply. And the wider our understanding becomes, the more easily and deeply we are able to forgive.

The passage ends with a beautiful definition of love: “⟦Q 174:1.5⟧Love is the outworking of the divine and inner urge of life. It is founded on understanding, nurtured by unselfish service, and perfected in wisdom.⟦/Q⟧” Love is not a momentary spark of emotion but a growing life. It begins from the root of understanding, feeds on the nourishment of service, and ripens into the fruit of wisdom. The Thought Adjuster within us helps this growth of love day by day. Such love is not perfected overnight, but it grows a little each day.

If someone comes to mind today whom you find hard to forgive, first try to understand them. Look with the Father’s eyes at why they acted as they did, and at what hurt and fear lay within them. Forgiveness may not come overnight, but the first step of trying to understand is already the beginning of love. The Father rejoices in that first step.
d335.pr: Think of one person you find hard to forgive, and write down the inner reasons that may have led them to act as they did.

msg: In his last discourse in the temple, Jesus made a final appeal for mercy to the Jewish leaders. But they rejected that appeal to the end, and that evening the Sanhedrin made its final decision to put Jesus to death. In recording this tragedy, the Urantia Book immediately sets apart a section to give its readers a solemn warning. That is today’s passage. Knowing how this event has been misused throughout history, the revelators could not pass over this point in silence.

The passage laments: “⟦Q 175:2.3⟧How cruel and unreasoning to compel innocent children to suffer for the sins of their progenitors, misdeeds of which they are wholly ignorant, and for which they could in no way be responsible!⟦/Q⟧” And it asks how wicked it is “⟦Q 175:2.3⟧to do such wicked deeds in the name of one who taught his disciples to love even their enemies!⟦/Q⟧” For many centuries countless professed Christians persecuted individual Jews, calling them the killers of Jesus. This was in direct opposition to the teachings of Jesus. That the name of the One who taught love has been used as a banner of hatred is one of the most painful ironies of history.

The revelators acknowledge that in recounting the life of Jesus they could not avoid recording that certain of his fellow Jews rejected him and brought about his death. But they declare plainly that such a historical recital “⟦Q 175:2.3⟧in no way justifies the unjust hatred⟦/Q⟧” toward individual Jews. It was particular leaders of a particular time who rejected Jesus, and to lay that responsibility on their descendants or on a whole people is neither justice nor truth. What is more, Jesus himself was a Jew, and his first apostles and disciples were all Jews. Sin is committed by individuals, and before God each person is responsible only for his own choices.

The passage says, “⟦Q 175:2.3⟧The Father and his Creator Son have never ceased to love the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 175:2.3⟧God is no respecter of persons, and salvation is for the Jew as well as for the gentile.⟦/Q⟧” This is a declaration that God’s love cannot be confined to any race or group. The heart of the gospel, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, denies at the root every form of collective hatred and prejudice.

This teaching puts a sharp question to us today as well. Are we lumping together and judging people of a certain race, religion, region, or political persuasion? Because of a wrong committed by one person, are we suspicious of or hostile toward everyone who belongs to the same group? Prejudice against a group keeps us from seeing the individual. And when that prejudice is justified in the name of faith, it takes on its most dangerous form. Prejudice usually grows out of fear and ignorance, and it loses its power before love and understanding.

Even on the cross, Jesus asked the Father to forgive those who were killing him. If we who call upon his name use that name to hate anyone, we reject him once again. Look honestly today to see whether any collective prejudice remains in your heart. And ask for eyes that see every person as a beloved child of the same Father. When those eyes are opened, we truly become the Master’s disciples.
d336.pr: Examine whether you have carelessly judged a whole group, and pray for one person who belongs to that group.

msg: On Tuesday evening on Mount Olivet, Jesus spoke of the destruction of Jerusalem and of his second coming. After they returned to the camp, the discussion with the apostles continued, and the Master told the parable of the talents, teaching about the responsibilities entrusted to believers. Today’s passage extends that teaching to the stewardship of truth. It begins with a short and powerful declaration: “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧Truth is living.⟦/Q⟧” This declaration gives the fundamental direction for how we are to treat truth.

The passage says that “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧the Spirit of Truth is ever leading the children of light into new realms of spiritual reality and divine service.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧You are not given truth to crystallize into settled, safe, and honored forms.⟦/Q⟧” Truth is not a relic to be kept in a museum but a growing life. The revelation of truth we have received must be so enhanced by passing through our personal experience that new beauty and actual spiritual gains will be disclosed to all who behold our spiritual fruits. What is living grows, and what grows changes. Yet even amid that change, the essence of the life carries on unbroken.

The passage then describes a truly sorry sight: successive generations of the professed followers of Jesus boasting that they have faithfully preserved the truth the Master committed to them, losing nothing and allowing no changes to be made. This is exactly like the servant who buried his talent in the ground and returned it just as it was. Outwardly it looks like loyalty, but in truth it is spiritual indolence that avoids the labor of living the truth and making it grow. The passage states firmly that such a plea “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧will not justify the barren steward of truth in the presence of the Master.⟦/Q⟧” Preservation is only the starting point, not the destination.

This teaching shows the difference between guarding faith and living it. Many religious traditions have regarded preserving doctrine in its original form as the highest loyalty. Certainly a heart that treasures truth is precious. But if we only guard truth like a fossil, that truth no longer transforms anyone. Elsewhere, too, the Urantia Book warns that when we try to confine divine truth within formulas or creeds, truth quickly dies (see Paper 180). Living truth always bears new fruit.

What, then, is the way to keep truth alive? It is to test and apply the truth we have received in daily experience, coming to understand it more deeply through that experience. The truth of God’s love deepens when we actually love someone. The truth of forgiveness comes alive only when we actually forgive. The passage says that “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧only those faithful servants who thus grow in the knowledge of the truth, and who thereby develop the capacity for divine appreciation of spiritual realities, can ever hope to ‘enter fully into the joy of their Lord.’⟦/Q⟧” Truth becomes ours not when we merely know it with our heads, but only when we live it with our hands and feet.

We who read the Urantia Book also stand before this warning. Accumulating much knowledge and memorizing passages is not enough. Live out in your life today one truth you have read. Then truth will become not a sentence in a book but a life growing within you, and the Master of truth will rejoice in its fruit. That is the faithful steward’s reckoning for the truth committed to him.
d337.pr: Choose one truth you have recently come to understand, and live it out today in concrete action.

d338.t: A Home of Love and Wisdom
msg: On Wednesday of the final week in Jerusalem, Jesus took a day of rest and went alone into the hills, and the lad John Mark followed him, carrying a lunch basket. That day the two talked long about this world and the next, and about home life. The Master praised John Mark for having grown up in a home ruled by love and wisdom, and so having acquired a strong and steady character. Today’s passage is a deep reflection that the author of the Urantia Book adds on the basis of that conversation. Jesus himself had grown up as the eldest son in the home at Nazareth and, after losing his father, had cared for the whole family, so he knew better than anyone the preciousness of the home.

The passage says that “⟦Q 177:2.6⟧the gospel of Jesus’ teaching, founded as it is on the father-child relationship, can hardly enjoy a world-wide acceptance until such a time as the home life of the modern civilized peoples embraces more of love and more of wisdom.⟦/Q⟧” This is a remarkable insight. The way we understand God as Father is greatly influenced by the parents we have known. To someone raised in a loveless home, the words that God is a loving Father may sound strange. On the other hand, a child who has known wise and warm parents can easily believe in the love of the heavenly Father.

The passage points out that although parents of the twentieth century possess great knowledge and increased truth, “⟦Q 177:2.6⟧very few modern homes are such good places in which to nurture boys and girls as Jesus’ home in Galilee and John Mark’s home in Judea.⟦/Q⟧” Much knowledge does not by itself make a good home. What makes a good home is not information but love and wisdom, together with consistent discipline and faith. The home of Jesus was poor, but within it lived respect for one another and reverence for God. The greatest gift parents can give their children is not great wealth, but the assurance of being loved and an example of trusting God.

But the passage also offers hope. It says that “⟦Q 177:2.6⟧the acceptance of Jesus’ gospel will result in the immediate improvement of home life.⟦/Q⟧” And it says that “⟦Q 177:2.6⟧the love life of a wise home and the loyal devotion of true religion exert a profound reciprocal influence upon each other.⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 177:2.6⟧Such a home life enhances religion, and genuine religion always glorifies the home.⟦/Q⟧” Home and faith are two roots that nourish each other. The love learned at home deepens faith, and deepened faith in turn warms the home.

This teaching leads us to look at our own homes today. Is our home a place where love rules and wisdom governs? In our busy daily lives, have we diligently taught our children knowledge and skills while neglecting to teach them the love of God and how to respect one another? These words apply also to those without children. Making the people we live with and the small communities we belong to into places of love and wisdom is everyone’s part. There is no perfect home, but there are homes that grow a little each day toward love and wisdom.

The home is the smallest unit of the kingdom of heaven. Even the great work of changing the world begins in the end at the table of a single home. In your time with your family today, listen a little more, be a little more patient, and express a little more gratitude. A home tended in this way becomes the most convincing evidence of the Father’s love to the world.
d338.pr: Today, give one specific word of thanks to a family member or someone you live with.

d339.t: The Gospel of the Living Seed
msg: On Thursday, the day before the cross, Jesus gave a last discourse to about fifty trusted followers at the camp near Gethsemane, on sonship in the kingdom and citizenship in the world. In this discourse the Master taught how believers should relate to secular governments and how they should live in the world. Toward the end of that discourse, the Master spoke of the nature of the gospel he was leaving behind: “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧This gospel of the kingdom is a living truth.⟦/Q⟧” These words are a kind of last testament, making clear how the gospel was to be carried on after the Master left the world.

The Master had earlier likened the gospel to the leaven in the dough and to the grain of mustard seed. Now he declares that it is “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧like the seed of the living being.⟦/Q⟧” A seed carries the same life from generation to generation, yet that life unfolds itself each time in new manifestations. An apple seed always becomes an apple tree, but the shape of the tree differs somewhat according to the soil and climate in which it grows. So too the gospel, while its essence does not change, grows anew to meet the needs of each age and each individual. Life carries itself forward not by copying but by growing.

The Master said, “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧The revelation I have made to you is a living revelation,⟦/Q⟧” and that he desired it to bear appropriate fruits in each individual and in each generation “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧in accordance with the laws of spiritual growth, increase, and adaptative development.⟦/Q⟧” This means that the gospel is not a fixed system of doctrine but a growing life. The application needed by the people of Galilee two thousand years ago may differ from the application we need today. But the core of that life, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, does not change. Each generation, therefore, does not merely inherit the gospel but bears the responsibility of living it anew in the language and life of its own time.

The Master said that “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧from generation to generation this gospel must show increasing vitality and exhibit greater depth of spiritual power.⟦/Q⟧” And he urged that “⟦Q 178:1.15⟧it must not be permitted to become merely a sacred memory, a mere tradition about me and the times in which we now live.⟦/Q⟧” This warning applies to the religion of every age. When faith stops at reminiscing about past glories, it becomes not a living seed but a dried specimen. This is the same reason the Urantia Book says elsewhere, again and again, that truth is living (see Paper 176).

This teaching leads us to examine our attitude toward faith. Do we remember Jesus merely as a great figure of history, or do we meet him as One who lives and works within us today through the Spirit of Truth? If the gospel is alive within us, it will continually renew our thoughts, habits, and relationships. There should be traces of spiritual growth between who I was last year and who I am this year. That growth shows itself more often in small, steady changes than in dramatic events.

A seed grows when it is planted in the ground and receives water and sunlight. The seed of the gospel also grows as we commune with the Father and serve our neighbors each day. Look today for the places in your life where the gospel is newly sprouting. And tend that small shoot with care so that it grows well. God waits patiently until that shoot becomes a great tree.
d339.pr: Look back on how your faith has grown and changed over the past year, and write down one thing for which you are grateful.

d340.t: The Master Who Washed Their Feet
msg: When the apostles entered the upper room for the Last Supper, they quarreled over their places. Feelings were hurt over who would sit beside the Master and who would have the higher seat. By Jewish custom, washing the guests’ feet before a meal was the task of a servant, but there was no servant present, and none of the apostles was willing to do it. Then the Master rose, laid aside his outer garment, girded himself with a towel, and began to wash the apostles’ feet one by one. Today’s passage is what the Master said after he had finished. That night this act was engraved on the apostles’ hearts as a scene they would never forget as long as they lived.

The Master first asks, “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧Do you really understand what I have done to you?⟦/Q⟧” Saying that they did well to call him Master, he asks, “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧If, then, the Master has washed your feet, why was it that you were unwilling to wash one another’s feet?⟦/Q⟧” This question was less a rebuke than a mirror held up to their hearts. The apostles revered the Master highly, yet they considered serving one another beneath their dignity. The Master laid bare the very root of that pride. He did not seek to shame the apostles, but led them to realize it for themselves.

The Master says, “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧A servant is not greater than his master; neither is one who is sent greater than he who sends him.⟦/Q⟧” If the Creator Son of a universe stooped to wash the dusty feet of his disciples, there is no reason why those who follow him cannot serve one another. The Master said, “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧You have seen the way of service in my life among you, and blessed are you who will have the gracious courage so to serve.⟦/Q⟧” Service requires courage, for it takes great courage to lay down our pride and step down to the lowly place. The Master did not teach service by words alone; he showed it by doing it himself.

The final question of the passage applies to us today just as it is: “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧But why are you so slow to learn that the secret of greatness in the spiritual kingdom is not like the methods of power in the material world?⟦/Q⟧” In the world, greatness is measured by how many people one rules. But in the kingdom of God, greatness is measured by how many people one serves. The apostles had been with the Master for more than three years, yet even on that last night they had not fully grasped this truth. This truth takes longer to learn with the body than to know with the head.

We too are slow learners. Even within churches and communities, we are easily captivated by position, office, and recognition. When there is some unpleasant task that someone must do, we wait for another to do it. But the Master’s way is to do that unpleasant task first. When we willingly take on work that no one wants and no one notices, we follow in the Master’s footsteps. In the place of service, competition disappears and brotherhood grows.

Look today for what washing someone’s feet might mean around you. It may be washing the dishes, quietly covering a coworker’s mistake, or carrying someone’s burden for them. When we serve in such lowly places, we taste the true greatness of the kingdom of God. That place is the very place where the Master stands.
d340.pr: Find one small unpleasant task today that no one wants to do, and quietly do it first.

msg: After the Last Supper, Jesus gave his farewell discourse to the eleven apostles. At its very beginning, the Master gave them a new commandment: that they love one another as he had loved them. And the Master said that he would no longer call them servants but friends. Today’s passage, explaining this teaching, makes clear what Jesus asks of his disciples: “⟦Q 180:1.6⟧It is loyalty, not sacrifice, that Jesus demands.⟦/Q⟧” These words are brief, yet they make us ask again, at the root, what the driving force of the religious life ought to be.

These words overturn the thinking of many religious people. We often think of the religious life as a path of sacrifice, of giving things up and enduring. But the passage says that “⟦Q 180:1.6⟧the consciousness of sacrifice implies the absence of that wholehearted affection which would have made such a loving service a supreme joy.⟦/Q⟧” When we do something for someone we love, we do not feel it as a sacrifice. The feeling of sacrifice may be a sign that we do not yet wholly love the one we serve.

The passage treats the idea of duty in the same way: “⟦Q 180:1.6⟧The idea of duty signifies that you are servant-minded and hence are missing the mighty thrill of doing your service as a friend and for a friend.⟦/Q⟧” Duty may be a necessary starting point, but it is not the goal of faith. Service done from duty is heavy and wearying, but service that comes from friendship is light and joyful. The passage says that “⟦Q 180:1.6⟧the impulse of friendship transcends all convictions of duty, and the service of a friend for a friend can never be called a sacrifice.⟦/Q⟧” God desires a friend who walks with him in joy rather than a servant dragged along against his will.

The last sentence of the passage shows how the relationship between Jesus and his disciples had grown. The Master first taught them that they were the sons of God, then called them brethren, and now, before he leaves, he calls them his friends. Sons, brethren, friends: these three names are steps of ever-deepening intimacy. Friends understand and trust one another and gladly stand together without expecting anything in return. What astonishing grace it is that the sovereign of a universe should call mortals his friends! The name of friend means that we no longer receive God’s will merely as a command, but have become companions who understand that will together and rejoice in it.

This teaching leads us to examine our religious life. Have praying, serving, and giving at some point become heavy duties? When you do something for God, do you feel that you are losing out? If so, rather than multiplying deeds, we must first restore the relationship. When we spend time with the Master as friends, service becomes joy once more. When the relationship comes alive, the deeds follow of themselves.

What the Master desires is not our grim sacrifice but unchanging loyalty, the heart of a friend who stays by his side to the end. Today, do what you do for God not as a duty but as a joy for a friend. That change of heart will transform our faith from a heavy and weary religion into a living friendship. Within that friendship we receive the strength to walk on to the end without growing weary.
d341.pr: Take one task of faith you have been doing out of duty, and today do it gladly as the Master’s friend.

msg: In the farewell discourse Jesus promised that after his departure he would send the Spirit of Truth. That spirit, he said, would lead believers into all truth. In explaining this promise, the Urantia Book offers a deep commentary on the very nature of truth, and today’s passage stands at its heart: “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧Divine truth is a spirit-discerned and living reality.⟦/Q⟧” This one sentence holds the whole of the right attitude toward truth. The Spirit of Truth is not a teacher who hands us answers from outside; he is the one who makes truth come alive within us.

The passage says that truth “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧exists only on high spiritual levels of the realization of divinity and the consciousness of communion with God.⟦/Q⟧” Truth is not the same as mere fact or information. Facts can be grasped by the intellect, but truth is fully discerned only within a living relationship with God. That is why the same words can become words of life to one reader and remain mere letters on a page to another. Coming to know truth is a matter of spiritual communion before it is ever a matter of knowledge.

The passage goes on: “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧You can know the truth, and you can live the truth; you can experience the growth of truth in the soul and enjoy the liberty of its enlightenment in the mind.⟦/Q⟧” Yet “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧you cannot imprison truth in formulas, codes, creeds, or intellectual patterns of human conduct.⟦/Q⟧” It warns that “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧when you undertake the human formulation of divine truth, it speedily dies.⟦/Q⟧” The moment we seize truth and shut it in a box, it is like pinning a butterfly as a specimen. The shape remains, but the life is gone. We must stay ever watchful, lest our zeal to guard the truth become the very thing that kills it.

Especially sharp are the words “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧Static truth is dead truth, and only dead truth can be held as a theory.⟦/Q⟧” The history of religion has been a repeated story of living experience hardening into doctrine and creed. At first there is a vivid experience of meeting God; in the next generation only the sentences describing that experience remain; and in the generation after that, only the arguments over defending those sentences. The Urantia Book warns again and again against such crystallization and insists that truth must always be experienced anew (see Paper 176).

The passage concludes: “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧Living truth is dynamic and can enjoy only an experiential existence in the human mind.⟦/Q⟧” This means that we do not possess truth; we live within it. Just as memorizing a definition of love is not knowing love, so arranging our concepts of God is not knowing God. As we live out the truth in our daily choices and relationships, the Spirit of Truth opens it to us ever more deeply and widely. The depth of truth, then, is shown not by how much we know but by how sincerely we live.

We who read the Urantia Book must therefore take care. We must not turn its teachings into yet another closed system, a tool for judging others. Do not stop at storing today’s truth in your head; ask the Spirit of Truth to let you experience it in your life. Only truth so experienced truly sets us free, and in that freedom we enjoy ever deeper communion with God.
d342.pr: Use the truth you have meditated on today not to teach others but to change one thing in the way you act.
